body: As important as some of the messages in The Social Reckoning are, the movie has been drastically underperforming at the box office. Per Variety, Aaron’s Sorkin’s follow up to The Social Network only grossed a measly $5.5 million this past weekend against a budget that’s somewhere within the $30–42 million range. That would make it a certifiable flop that’s costing Columbia Pictures (and Sony) quite a bit of money — especially when you compare it to The Social Network’s $22 million opening.
The Social Reckoning is flopping at the box office
Meanwhile, Other Mommy is having an unexpected moment.

This isn’t entirely surprising given how middling reviews for the film have been. It’s currently got a 55% rating on Rotten Tomatoes and has widely been trashed on social media. All of this might be reflective of audiences hoping for a proper sequel to The Social Network, which won three Oscars for its screenplay (written by Sorkin), editing, and score. But it might speak to people not fully clicking with Mikey Madison’s performance as whistleblower Frances Haugen or Jeremy Allen White’s turn as Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz. (Madison, for her part, indicated to The Hollywood Reporter that it was Sorkin’s vision as director that kept from “authentically and faithfully represent[ing] a real person,” which she hopes to do in the future.) It also probably didn’t help that Jesse Eisenberg — who portrayed Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network — had no interest in being in the film, according to Sorkin himself.

Ironically, Blumhouse’s Other Mommy raked in an impressive $27.5 million this weekend, which likely suggests that people are more interested in novel horror as opposed to reminders of how social media has made everyone’s lives worse.

articles.headline: DNC Chair Ken Martin defends 'Big Tent' strategy when pressed on democratic socialists
keyFacts: Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin defended the party's big-tent approach, arguing Democrats win by expanding their coalition.
The Republican National Committee criticized Martin, claiming he embraces far-left radicals who want to abolish police, prisons, and borders.
A White House report estimated that adopting seven major democratic socialist policies would add 49 trillion dollars to federal deficits.
body: Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin defended his party's big-tent approach Monday, arguing Democrats must continue expanding their coalition even as Republicans target the party over its ties to democratic socialists.
Martin was pressed during an interview on MSNOW about whether the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is a liability for the party ahead of the midterm elections .

"So let me just say, I've always taken a big-tent approach to how you build a party," Martin said. "That's why I was successful for all these years in Minnesota. I believe you win through addition, not subtraction. You win by growing your coalition, not shrinking it."
NEWSOM TELLS DEMOCRATS TO BE IN THE 'ADDITION NOT SUBTRACTION' BUSINESS WITH SOCIALISTS
"And sometimes, is there a middle ground, though, when Americans see that…" interjected MSNOW anchor Peter Alexander.

"No, not at all, because that's where the vast majority of Americans are at," Martin replied. "Maybe right in the middle, or a little center-left, or a little center-right. But it doesn't mean we can't bring new voices into the party, right? Of course, we have to keep growing and we have to keep expanding this tent," Martin reiterated.
SEE IT: TOP DEM OPERATIVE DRAWS LINE AT ‘DEPLORABLE’ HASAN PIKER AFTER TOUTING PARTY’S ‘BIG TENT’
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Democratic National Committee for comment.
"Democratic Party Chair Ken Martin embraces far-Left radicals who want to abolish the police, prisons, and borders," the Republican National Committee wrote on X.
DSA CO-CHAIR MOCKED FOR PROUDLY CONFIRMING SOCIALISTS WANT TO ABOLISH THE SENATE, NATIONAL BORDERS, PRISONS

The DSA has advocated far-left policies, including abolishing police, prisons and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), as well as eliminating immigration restrictions and expanding public ownership.

President Donald Trump and Republicans have frequently targeted the DSA ahead of the November elections. Earlier this month, Trump's Council of Economic Advisers released a report estimating that adopting seven major DSA policies would add $49 trillion to federal deficits over 10 years, equivalent to more than $350,000 per American household.
SEN MARK KELLY WARNS FAR-LEFT POLICIES THAT ‘DON’T MAKE SENSE’ COULD COST DEMOCRATS SEATS

"Make no mistake, these are the Democrats’ policies," a White House news release regarding the report stated. "They want to destroy our great, hard-fought nation, and plummet our economy and the very fabric of our nation into the ground."
Meanwhile, many mainstream Democrats have tried to distance themselves from the DSA label, pointing to their support for capitalism and social democracy.

articles.headline: Energy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine
keyFacts: Oil and gas prices rose after President Donald Trump's announced energy ceasefire failed to stop Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine received no advance warning of the ceasefire, while the Kremlin neither confirmed nor denied agreeing to it.
Russia said it would lift some export restrictions to accommodate a diesel deal with Trump, though the timing remains unclear.
body: Oil and gas prices rose Monday after an “energy ceasefire” announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday failed to gain traction.
Brent crude oil jumped 2% to almost $108 per barrel and U.S. crude oil rose more than 2% to about $94. Meanwhile, diesel futures fully erased a small drop they saw last week.

Just weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the price pressures are mounting. Republicans face a steep climb to maintain their majorities in Congress, and voters across the country cite high gas prices as a key issue affecting their votes.
The average nationwide price of diesel fuel Monday was $6.26 per gallon, nearly 80% higher than it had been at the start of the year, according to AAA data.
The rising prices Monday came less than 24 hours after Trump declared that a ceasefire had been agreed to.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Shortly after the president’s post, Russia renewed strikes against Ukrainian energy assets.

Pressed by reporters Monday as to why neither the Kremlin nor Kyiv had firmly committed to his ceasefire, Trump indicated that he knew when he made the announcement on Sunday that he did not yet have a commitment from either side.

“They agreed, you know why? Because I said ‘You agree,” Trump told reporters at the White House. As for getting Russian President Vladimir Putin to commit, Trump said, “We’re going to see what happens.”
Asked if he was aware that Russia had already violated the ceasefire Trump had announced, the president replied, “I’m not sure about that,” before claiming there had been “violations on both sides.”
Ceasefire déjà vu

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine learned about Trump’s ceasefire from media reports and was given no advance warning. He reiterated his position that Ukraine was open to an agreement not to target enemy energy infrastructure as long as Moscow agrees to it, too.
In the meantime, Russia continued with “glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that a power plant in Kharkiv had recently been attacked.
“Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet,’” Zelenskyy said, using the Russian word for “no.”
The Kremlin on Monday neither confirmed nor denied having agreed to a deal.
Trump’s Sunday announcement closely mirrored a similar post he made in September, when he announced that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”

There, too, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s participation hinged on Russia’s agreement to comply, which never came. Neither Ukrainian nor Russian strikes on the other’s energy assets slowed down in September.
Trump’s deal with Putin

The dubious ceasefire Trump declared over the weekend followed a stunning announcement Friday in which the president said Russia would supply millions of barrels of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.”
The announcement came after a phone call Friday between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin that reportedly lasted over an hour.

Trump said the deal with Putin would “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” That would translate into about 2.25 million barrels of diesel, or less diesel than the United States uses in just one day.
Further details and logistics of Russia’s plan had yet to be announced Monday.
In addition to the Russia deal, Trump has pressured G7 allies to release more diesel fuel supplies in recent days and lifted domestic restrictions on an off-road variety of diesel.
In order to clear a legal path for the diesel deal, the Treasury Department announced a six-month suspension of the fuel sanctions imposed on the Kremlin in 2022 for its illegal invasion of Ukraine.
Ukrainian officials, European allies and some U.S. lawmakers were aghast at the deal and the U.S. decision to unilaterally ease Russia sanctions.
Trump defended the deal Monday, calling it “the right choice for the American People.”
Trump also said more diesel fuel would be made available “within a short period of time,” if Russia’s refineries could produce it.
Questions about Russia’s capacity
Yet experts are highly skeptical that there will be any significant resumption of Russian diesel exports in the near term.
Due to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia, refiners that produce oil, gas and diesel have suffered heavy damage.

“Reported gasoline output is down by 20% compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%, prompting the government to restrict fuel exports to protect domestic supplies,” analysts at the International Energy Agency wrote in a September report.
For weeks, Trump has focused on the price of diesel fuel, which began rising as a result of the Iran war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
In July, escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war began adding to the pressure on diesel prices.
As Ukrainian drones systematically targeted Russian energy assets, the Kremlin responded by restricting diesel exports in order to preserve its supply for domestic use.
Until then, Russia had been one of the world’s top exporters of refined oil products, which include diesel fuel.
Russia said Friday that it would lift some of its export restrictions in order to accommodate the deal with Trump. But it was unclear how fast that would happen.

articles.headline: Tim Burton Horror Lives In Weird Steam Adventure That Reminds Me Of The Creepiest 2010s Games
keyFacts: Indie developer Miss Self Destruct released a new trailer for the psychological horror game Hell Is Other People at the Cozy After Dark Showcase.
The Steam description states that players manage social skills instead of inventory items, responding to a mother character's comments with emotions like Guilt.
Players must consult a notebook to manage shifting emotions and figure out how normal people behave.
body: My 2012 belonged to Slender Man. I was easily terrified by creepy, early 2010s computer games like Slender: The Eight Pages, but I couldn't resist their special blend of unicorn blood and twee. Recently, I've been missing the pink bittersweetness of the Tim Burton-style horror games made in those years, like Fran Bow and Alice: Madness Returns , so the inaugural Cozy After Dark Showcase has arrived with a new trailer for Hell Is Other People at just the right time.

The teaser from indie developer Miss Self Destruct describes Hell Is Other People--named for the famous Jean-Paul Sartre quote about being trapped in other people's perceptions of you--as "a psychological horror about social anxiety."

Its little girl protagonist has onyx eyes and hair that goes nearly down to her fingertips, so she looks a bit overgrown, like she might have washed up on some riverbank. Otherwise, she seems normal, with a thin mattress to curl on top of every night like any other lonely child. But that's not what her mother thinks.
https://youtu.be/7VJ07UqoUyI?si=UM_03yezg2sQ1YA-&t=3530

"See what I have to deal with?" Mother says as our little girl stares politely at a party tray of frosted cupcakes. Hell Is Other People's Steam description explains that you won't collect items in your inventory, but social skills, so the girl responds to her mother's snide comment with Guilt--but it isn't impactful. She becomes paranoid, making lines of dialogue seem to jumble and melt together as the girl explains, "When I feel bad, people become so hard to read."

You'll have to manage these shifting tides of emotion by consulting your notebook for how normal people behave. Initially, I was drawn to the pretty Gothic caricature of Hell Is Other People, black cats with sharp syringe teeth and patterned arsenic wallpaper, but now I'm feeling understood by it as a true social survival game.

When I myself was a strange girl with long hair that blew around on the swingsets, I was much like the Hell Is Other People protagonist; I was desperate for my parents to understand me, and I couldn't understand why they didn't try. My only solace in those years was Tim Burton's corpse bride and monsters like Slender Man--outcasts. It can be pleasant to give up and call yourself a freak, exist among freaks. So I'm excited for the gloomy nostalgia Hell Is Other People brings me when it's out sometime soon.

articles.headline: Democrats rebuke federal raid of Ilhan Omar’s home: ‘rogue abuse of power’
keyFacts: Federal agents searched Minnesota Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar's home on Monday morning.
Fox News reported that the search pertained to a criminal fraud investigation regarding Omar's childhood immigration paperwork.
House Democratic leaders condemned the search and vowed to deliver full accountability from federal law enforcement departments.
body: Ilhan Omar’s Democratic colleagues have condemned federal agents’ search of the Minnesota congresswoman’s home on Monday morning, describing it as “deeply disturbing” and emblematic of the Trump administration’s “corrupt weaponization” of the US government.
House Democratic leaders, including minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, party whip Katherine Clark and caucus chair Pete Aguilar, issued a joint statement excoriating the president for the search.

“The Trump administration’s raid on congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against [the president’s] adversaries,” their statement said.

“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations. Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected member of Congress and her family.”

The Democratic leaders vowed to “deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power” from the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, the latter of which oversees immigration enforcement.

Citing unnamed sources “close to the investigation”, Fox News – which is typically friendly with the Trump administration – reported that the search on Omar’s home pertained to a criminal fraud investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Omar’s late father filled out that paperwork when Omar, a Somali-born, naturalized US citizen, was a child.

California representative Ro Khanna also condemned Monday’s search, saying: “It is simply chilling that they are targeting political opponents this way, and it is disturbing that they are targeting Muslim Americans and a Muslim American legislator. Any decent American needs to stand up and speak out.”
Sydney Kamlager-Dove, Khanna’s fellow Democrat and California representative, called the search “fascism in the extreme”.

“This is an unadulterated abuse of power,” Kamlager-Dove said. “Trump is weaponizing the federal government to escalate his racist attacks against [representative] Omar, undermine her ahead of the midterms [on 3 November], and distract from his failures as president.”

Pramila Jayapal, a Democratic House member from Washington state, similarly called the search of Omar’s home a “disgusting abuse of power from an out of control president” facing widespread public disapproval from high living costs amid the war in Iran that he helped start alongside Israel in February.

“To use federal law enforcement resources to raid the home of a sitting Member of Congress weeks before an election is a dangerous sign of an authoritarian president who will stop at nothing to distract you from his deep unpopularity with the American people,” Jayapal added.

Jayapal’s statement alluded to years of unsubstantiated rumors from Trump and others about Omar and her family, including the accusation that her ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, is in fact her brother – and that the marriage was part of an effort to earn him immigration status. Omar has denied those rumors.

The Illinois representative Delia C Ramirez called for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to be dismantled. Omar “has not backed down, so now they are using DHS and the federal government to target and persecute her”, Ramirez said in a post on X.
“This is an absolute abuse of power and unacceptable. We must strip them of their weapons. We must dismantle DHS.”

Similarly, Greg Casar, a Democratic representative from Texas, wrote that the Trump administration is targeting Omar “because he thinks it’ll help his [Republican] party” during the midterms, when it is expected to lose seats in Congress.
“Ilhan Omar stands up and won’t let Trump do whatever he wants to our country,” Casar said. “It’s up to us to do the same.”

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the US’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, also spoke out against the search of Omar’s home, saying: “We strongly condemn this unconscionable raid on her home for what it is: an obvious act of political persecution.”

Criticizing the Trump administration’s handling of files pertaining to Jeffrey Epstein’s child sex-trafficking network as well as the president’s pardons for those who attacked the US Capitol in early 2021, Cair said the justice department “could clearly [not] care less about fighting crime and is instead focused on conducting a witch hunt”.

articles.headline: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
keyFacts: Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on Monday as its first frontier artificial intelligence models.
Meta stated that the new models achieve benchmark scores comparable to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
Meta researchers emphasized the models' active memory feature designed to retain user information over long periods.
body: Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.

Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.
Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”

To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.

“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.

The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year. Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio, which came online earlier this year.

articles.headline: Microsoft blames a configuration change for Exchange Admin Center tumble
keyFacts: Microsoft experienced an outage of the Exchange Admin Center caused by a recent configuration change that resulted in internal server and redirect errors.
Administrators were temporarily unable to access the management console because Microsoft stated there was no workaround available during the incident.
Microsoft resolved the outage by rolling back the configuration change and stated it is reviewing its change processes and monitoring tools.
body: Microsoft took down the Exchange Admin Center (EAC) today after a code change left administrators facing an "Internal Server Error" when trying to access the service. Microsoft first admitted that something was amiss at 0937 UTC on October 12, noting, "When attempting to access the Exchange admin center, affected admins may encounter an 'Internal Server Error' message." Any administrator attempting to access the EAC could be affected. It was more than an hour before the company stated: "We've identified unexpected 302 redirect errors during affected Exchange admin center (EAC) access attempts and are analyzing diagnostic logs to isolate the source of the access failures. "While we continue our investigation, admins remain unable to access the EAC, with no workaround currently available." So, a fun morning for Microsoft's European users. According to Microsoft, the EAC is "a modern, web-based management console for managing Exchange Online." Want to manage mailboxes? EAC is where you go. Group management? Again, EAC. Microsoft explained: "The design of the EAC in Exchange Online aligns with the overall Microsoft 365 admin experience." Sadly, that alignment appears to extend to service wobbles caused by changes rolled out without due care and attention. Two hours after admitting things had gone awry, Microsoft said it was "continuing to test the rollback of the recent Exchange admin center (EAC) change while monitoring the results to determine if this resolves the impact." At this point, administrators were nodding sagely at an all-too familiar story. Of course rolling back the change did the trick. Microsoft stated as much in its final update: "A recent EAC configuration change resulted in unexpected HTTP responses within the affected request path, preventing admins from successfully accessing the EAC. "Reverting the identified change restored expected service functionality." Microsoft also assured customers it was reviewing the change to ensure it didn't make the same mistake again, as well as its monitoring and telemetry, to "improve detection and alerting for similar service behavior." The problem is that this is hardly a new phenomenon. In September, Microsoft made a configuration change that left some users unable to access SharePoint Online sites and pages. In April, another ill-thought-through change took down Outlook for iOS. And, in 2025, Microsoft 365 tumbled from the cloud because of yet another configuration change. It's almost as if testing changes consists of little more than asking Copilot, "does this look alright to you?" and then hitting the go button. The latest outage was resolved before the end of the working day, and a preliminary Post-Incident Report is due within two business days, with a final report due next week. Hopefully one or the other will contain words along the lines of "Hey, this keeps happening, maybe we should do some more testing before deploying to production?" ®
